speaking.q: Do you think hope can genuinely change the way people deal with difficult situations, or is it sometimes just a form of unrealistic thinking?
If hope is more than simply wanting something to happen, what do you think turns hope into something practical and useful?
Even with a good plan, people inevitably experience failure. What determines whether someone recovers from a setback or gives up?
Why do some people treat failure as useful information, while others see it as proof that they are not capable enough?
If our own thinking affects hope, how much influence do the people around us have on whether we remain hopeful?
Can being hopeful make people more willing to take risks and pursue ambitious goals?
If something genuinely cannot be changed, should we continue hoping, or is there a point at which we need to accept reality?
At what point can hope stop being helpful and begin to prevent people from making realistic decisions?
Do you think hope is mainly part of someone's personality, or can people deliberately become more hopeful?
Taking everything we have discussed into account, to what extent do you believe hope can actually influence the future we create for ourselves?
If hope encourages us to take action, how should we deal with situations in which the outcome is largely beyond our control?
If we cannot know what the future will bring, is uncertainty an enemy of hope or actually a necessary part of it?
Why are some people able to work towards a distant goal for years, while others give up when results do not appear quickly?
We often tell people that hope and effort can change their lives. But are there circumstances in which determination simply is not enough?
If circumstances influence hope, what responsibility do leaders have for making other people feel that improvement is possible?
Can hope help repair damaged relationships, or can hoping that someone will change sometimes keep us in unhealthy situations?
Do you think believing that you will succeed can actually improve your performance, even when your ability has not changed?
So far we have mainly discussed personal hope. Can entire communities or societies become more hopeful or more hopeless?
If people invest a great deal of hope in a particular future and it never happens, how can they recover without becoming cynical?
After considering optimism, failure, uncertainty, social barriers and acceptance, how would you now define a healthy and mature form of hope?
